subject: Culture
title: Graduation Origins
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Graduation Origins.

hook.text: The graduation cap and gown come from medieval monks. Universities started in monasteries.

buildup.text: The cap—mortarboard—represents the scholar's authority. The gown marks separation from the common crowd.

discovery.text: Throwing the cap started at the US Naval Academy in 1912, when graduates no longer needed their midshipman hats.

twist.text: In many countries, graduation isn't celebrated. German students finish quietly. The American ceremony is the outlier.

climax.text: Graduation works as ritual because it's public. The community witnesses the transformation.

punchline.text: The hat flies because the old self is gone.

quiz.question: Where did the tradition of throwing graduation caps originate?

details.summary: Academic graduation ceremonies descend from medieval European universities where scholars wore clerical robes and mortarboards. The cap, gown, and ceremonial walk were originally practical religious clothing, not symbols — but centuries of tradition transformed them into powerful markers of.
details.whyItMatters: Graduation is the modern world's most widespread rite of passage. Understanding its medieval religious origins reveals how secular rituals inherit and repurpose sacred ceremony structures.
takeaways: Academic regalia originated from medieval clerical dress
The mortarboard cap may derive from the biretta worn by Catholic clergy
Graduation ceremonies are practiced nearly identically worldwide

faq.question: Why do graduates wear caps and gowns?
faq.answer: Medieval scholars were members of the clergy and wore robes for warmth in drafty stone buildings. The gown became standardized as academic dress when universities formalized in the 12th-13th centuries. The mortarboard may derive from the clerical biretta or mason's board.

faq.question: When did graduation ceremonies start?
faq.answer: The earliest known commencement ceremonies date to the University of Bologna and University of Paris in the 12th-13th centuries. The word 'commencement' means 'beginning' — it marked the start of a scholar's professional career.
